Why this work matters

The human side of digital transformation

AI transformation succeeds when technology, people, learning, and organizational systems are developed together.

Digital transformation is usually funded as a technology project. In practice, it succeeds or stalls on human capability. When people do not know when, how and why to use a tool, it does not change how work gets done.

  1. Technology needs workforce readiness

    Licences and platforms create opportunity. Results come only when staff can use them confidently in their own roles.

  2. AI tools alone do not guarantee productivity

    Gains depend on good task selection, verifying outputs, and redesigning workflows. Access alone does not deliver them.

  3. Role-specific pathways matter

    A finance officer, an HR officer and a policy analyst use AI differently. One generic course cannot serve them all.

  4. Training must be measurable

    Effective programmes combine assessment, practical application, ongoing support and outcome indicators. Attendance is not enough.

  5. Responsible use is a skill

    Human judgement, privacy safeguards and awareness of governance must be taught and checked. They cannot be assumed.

Proposed framework

Public Service AI Capability Framework

Five learning levels, from individual AI literacy to sustained organizational performance.

This is an illustrative consulting framework, offered for possible adaptation by the Ministry. It is not an adopted government framework.

  1. Level 1 · Understand

    AI Foundations

    • AI literacy
    • Capabilities & limitations
    • Responsible use
    • Data privacy
    • Human oversight

    Outcome: Explains what AI can and cannot do, and when not to use it.

  2. Level 2 · Use

    AI Productivity

    • Drafting
    • Summarisation
    • Research support
    • Communication
    • Everyday knowledge work

    Outcome: Uses approved tools safely for routine tasks and verifies every output.

  3. Level 3 · Apply

    Role-Specific Application

    • Administrative staff
    • Human resources
    • Finance
    • Policy development
    • Managers & departments

    Outcome: Applies AI to the real tasks and rules of their own role.

  4. Level 4 · Improve

    Advanced AI-Enabled Workflows

    • Workflow redesign
    • AI-assisted analysis
    • Automation concepts
    • Evaluation
    • Responsible implementation

    Outcome: Redesigns team processes and evaluates AI use against risks and benefits.

  5. Level 5 · Sustain

    Sustainable Adoption & Performance

    • Competency validation
    • Performance support
    • Coaching
    • Analytics & adoption monitoring
    • Continuous improvement

    Outcome: Capability is validated, supported and improved over time.

Across every levelPrivacy & data protectionAccuracy & verificationConfidentialityHuman accountability

Individual awareness→ increasing capability and organizational impact →Sustained performance

A final framework would be built through stakeholder consultation and aligned with existing Ministry initiatives, such as the National AI Literacy Initiative. It would also be based on a formal training needs assessment.

Sample learning experience · 5–7 minutes

AI for Public Service Productivity: Responsible Use in Everyday Work

An interactive demonstration of my instructional design, using a fictional scenario and synthetic data.

It is mapped to Framework Levels 1–2 (Foundations & Productivity). Learners work through:

  1. A realistic public service scenario with five everyday AI decisions
  2. A review of an AI-generated draft that contains hidden errors
  3. A safeguards check and a five-question knowledge assessment
  4. Formative feedback and a competency completion indicator

Proposed 90-day pilot

Public Service AI Workforce Readiness and Learning Design Pilot

This is an illustrative proposal. The scope, staffing, systems access and schedule would all need to be agreed with the Ministry.

  1. Phase 1 · Days 1–20

    Discover

    Discovery, stakeholder engagement, training needs assessment and capability baseline.

    • Stakeholder map and interview summary
    • Training needs assessment instrument and findings
    • AI capability baseline for pilot cohorts
  2. Phase 2 · Days 21–45

    Design

    Competency framework, role-specific pathways, curriculum prototypes and assessment design.

    • Draft competency framework (adapted Levels 1–5)
    • Two or three role-specific pathway outlines
    • Prototype modules and scenario-based assessments
  3. Phase 3 · Days 46–70

    Deliver

    Training delivery, user testing, performance support and feedback.

    • Pilot delivery to agreed cohorts
    • Job aids and performance-support resources
    • Mid-pilot feedback and usability findings
  4. Phase 4 · Days 71–90

    Evaluate

    Evaluation, adoption analysis, refinement and scale-up recommendations.

    • Pilot evaluation report
    • Refined modules and framework
    • Scale-up roadmap and recommendations

Proposed indicators of success

These are proposed indicators, not achieved results. Targets would be set with the Ministry after the baseline.

Participation & completionEnrolment, attendance and module completion by cohort
Competency gainPre- and post-training competency against the framework
Scenario performanceResults on realistic, role-based assessment tasks
Appropriate AI useCorrect task selection and safeguard application
Employee confidenceSelf-reported confidence before and after
Tool adoptionUse of approved tools, where data is available
Workflow proficiencyObserved or self-reported proficiency on target workflows
Participant feedbackRelevance, quality and usefulness ratings
Scaling readinessEvidence-based recommendations for the next phase

Professional profile

Dr. Barbara Zá Franks, EdD

AI Learning Architect · Workforce Development Strategist · Digital Transformation Consultant
Education Executive · Learning Experience Designer · AI-Enabled Learning Systems Specialist

Dr. Barbara Zá Franks is a Bahamian education executive and AI learning architect based in Freeport, Grand Bahama. Over 18 years she has worked across K–12, online and international education, moving from the classroom to Chief Academic Officer of a multi-campus international school network.

She currently owns K–12 Language Arts programming for 50+ Alpha Schools campuses at 2 Hour Learning, with responsibility spanning curriculum, assessment, intervention, analytics and AI-generated learning systems, working alongside learning science, product and engineering teams. As Chief Research Officer (consulting) at Virtuous Sea Corporation, she leads applied research on workforce readiness and labour-market trends.

Earlier, she held executive roles with KnowledgeLink, including Chief Academic Officer, Regional Dean and Academic Dean. In those roles she led policy, quality assurance and faculty development across campuses in China and an online U.S. diploma program, and she later served as Head of School in Anguilla. She holds a Doctor of Education in Leadership.

She is committed to contributing her experience to national development: helping Bahamian institutions prepare their people for AI-driven change, responsibly and measurably.
